extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, literature students, and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Lecture-based guidance on the principal aspects by which novels should be written and judged (story, people, plot, fantasy, prophecy, pattern, rhythm, etc.), aimed at helping critics and novelists recognize virtues and anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the novel
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘A fiction in prose of a certain extent’ — Forster adopts Abel Chevalley’s definition and adds a working proviso that the extent should not be less than 50,000 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any fictitious prose work over 50,000 words will be treated as a novel in these lectures. Forster asks critics to accept this pragmatic boundary and to justify any alternative that would include or exclude specific long prose works (gives examples of borderline works).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Story (fundamental aspect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The story is 'a narrative of events arranged in their time sequence' and is the fundamental, backbone aspect of the novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a story it has one merit—making the audience want to know what happens next—and one fault—making the audience not want to know what happens next. The novelist must wield suspense (Scheherazade example). The story is the lowest common denominator of all novels and must not be confused with the higher artistic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: People / Characterization (flat vs round)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters (People) are a central aspect; Forster distinguishes between 'flat' characters and 'round' characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flat characters are constructed around a single idea or quality and can be easily summarized; they are useful and valid in fiction. Round characters are complex, capable of change and surprise. A novelist should choose and deploy flat or round characters according to design; evaluate characters by whether they sustain interest, surprise, and verisimilitude. Examples and contrasts are discussed throughout (many exemplars: Jane Austen, Thackeray, Sterne, Woolf).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (as distinct from story)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is more than chronological sequence; it is the arrangement of events to show causal relations and to build an organising structure or meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forster distinguishes plot from mere story (see index reference 'Plot defined'). Plotting creates causal expectation and may support pattern, but an over-rigid plot or artificial contrivance that sacrifices life or character for pattern is an anti-pattern. Evaluate plots for how naturally events arise from characters and for whether imposed causation enriches or impoverishes the novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view / Narrative perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Point of view (narrative stance and method) shapes the reader’s perception; technical features such as use of 'he said'/'she said' vary by period and influence effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of omniscience, limited perspective, free indirect style, or dialogue-reporting affects tone, intimacy, and reliability. Forster warns that differences in point-of-view technique can colour otherwise similar material; critics should attend to how point of view is executed and how it conditions reader response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy (technique and tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy is an aspect in which writers start from small objects or eccentricities and let the narrative flutter into digression and whimsical perception (Forster groups Woolf and Sterne as fantasists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fantasy combines humorous appreciation of life’s muddle with a sense of beauty and deliberate bewilderment. It is valuable when it achieves consistent tone and illuminates human experience; the anti-pattern is aimless digression that loses coherence or reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy (novel’s prophetic/visionary power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophecy refers to the novel’s capacity to foresee or propheticise social/psychological trends (Forster defines 'Prophecy' as an aspect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a novel genuinely anticipates or illuminates future human conditions or merely projects contemporary anxieties. Forster treats prophecy as a distinguishable mode worth examining for its philosophical or psychological reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern (external formal unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern denotes an imposed external form or rigid structural unity (hourglass, cathedral, converging/diverging lines) that shapes a novel’s material into a design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pattern can produce beauty but risks 'shutting the doors on life'—a rigid pattern may force life to be whittled or distorted to fit form (Forster cites James as extreme example). The anti-pattern is prioritising ingeniously rigid external form over living material; readers often feel 'beautifully done, but not worth doing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm (internal repetition + variation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm is repetition plus variation inside a book—an internal stitching (the 'little phrase' in Proust) that can give coherence and beauty without external patterning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forster distinguishes two kinds of rhythm: the easily perceptible repeating motifs/phrases (example: Vinteuil’s little phrase in Proust) which stitch a novel internally, and a more complex 'symphonic' rhythm (harder to identify). Rhythm should emerge organically, often spontaneously; when forced into symbol or repeated trivially it becomes boring. Rhythm may achieve beauty without mutilating characters; it is preferable to mechanical patterning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and narrative voice (colloquialism and register)
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel is often colloquial in tone; conversational words and a talkative tone may be appropriate to the form (Forster intentionally preserves colloquialities in the lectures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voice must suit the novel’s aims; colloquial, personal phrasing can reveal secrets of the form that grander criticism misses. Critics should expect and evaluate naturalness of voice rather than impose high-flown standards unsuited to the novel's colloquial energies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affection / Human test (final critical test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final test of a novel is 'our affection for it'—the human-to-human response; emotion and human feeling are integral and unavoidable in judging a novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism cannot exclude the intensely human quality of the novel. While sentimentality must be guarded against, complete exorcism of humanity makes the novel 'wilt.' The critic should balance emotional response with analytic judgement, but recognise personal affection as a legitimate and central test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read thoroughly; avoid pseudo-scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster warns against the pseudo-scholar who classifies and generalises without having read or properly assimilated books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and writers must read books closely rather than classifying by period, subject-matter, locality, or 'tendency' as a shortcut. Anti-patterns listed: mechanical classification by date/subject (e.g., 'novels about weather' with nine subtypes), over-reliance on the term 'genius' as a stopgap, and portable 'tendencies' used without reading. Genuine judgement requires close reading and struggle with the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid provincialism; maintain wide outlook
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics must not be provincially narrow; they have a duty to have a wide outlook and avoid mistaking local affection for universal importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forster urges critics to compare English fiction with the great continental achievements (Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, Proust) and to avoid acclaiming 'little mansions' as mighty edifices through parochial prejudice. A critic is required to see literature 'beyond time' and avoid narrowness of viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of detail and visualization (humour and social effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cataloguing concrete details and visualisation produce humour and social commentary (Forster compares Wells and Dickens as cataloguers and visualisers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such techniques generate lively surface effects and social indignation, and they can be socially valuable (reform-minded humour). Anti-patterns include lack of taste, over-prolixity, or the author's face drawing too near the reader—detail used without aesthetic discrimination can appear cheap or scratchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspiration and the creative state
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster notes the condition of inspiration as a common creative state across ages; the critic should account for inspiration rather than over-systematize it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'inspiration' as a real, informal force in creation; don't try to reduce all works to systems or historical tendencies. Recognise that many great effects arise from the novelist being 'approximated by the act of creation' rather than consciously following literary fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer expansion to completion (aesthetic aim)
rubrics_metrics.description: The desirable artistic movement in fiction is 'expansion'—opening out—rather than tight completion or rounding-off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forster suggests fiction should aim to expand the mind’s experience (analogy to symphony's expansion) rather than neatly complete or resolve everything; War and Peace is cited as an example where untidy material nonetheless produces large chords that sound behind the reader. Evaluate novels for their capacity to open perspective rather than close it artificially.
